question: Does any existing work construct a benchmark of amended statutes or regulations with near-duplicate successive revisions and time-stamped queries, which would pre-empt the proposed benchmark contribution?
description: Across the retrieved set, temporal benchmarks are ESG disclosures (TemporalESG), financial filings (TempFinQA), and web QA with dates (SituatedQA/TimeQA); regulatory-document work found so far is static (RMA reports, legal NLP datasets). No retrieved work was found that builds a benchmark of amended statutes/regulations with near-duplicate successive revisions, validity metadata, and time-stamped queries. Absence in the retrieved set is not proof of absence in the literature.
confidence_basis: Comparative evidence across five adjacent benchmarks plus a survey statement about the absence of temporally dynamic legal QA data; the verdict is limited to the searched set because the paper budget was exhausted and some sources returned rate-limit errors, so very recent or unindexed work cannot be excluded.
rationale: The survey states legal QA datasets are static and do not address temporal dynamics of legal knowledge, and the closest temporal benchmarks found are in ESG and financial domains.
resolution: Partially resolved: within the searched set, no directly matching work was found. No retrieved paper builds time-stamped queries over amended statutes/regulations with near-duplicate successive clause versions and version-level gold labels. The nearest work is a legal MCQA benchmark that encodes temporal validity and normative relationships but evaluates answer choice, not which version was retrieved; point-in-time financial QA over filings; a trilingual ESG-disclosure temporal benchmark; a regulatory-financial retrieval benchmark without any temporal dimension; and a linked-data versioning benchmark that measures storage/query performance. Caveats: searching was budget-limited (paper budget exhausted, some rate-limit errors), so recent or unindexed work cannot be excluded, and the closest legal benchmark may itself be extendable to version-level evaluation, which would further reduce the benchmark's novelty.
